lead: Nerve conduction velocity (NCV) is the speed of an action potential along a peripheral nerve, reported in metres per second (m/s). The measurement exists because a damaged nerve conducts slowly, and a doctor needs a number, not just a feeling that the limb is weak. The test stimulates the same nerve at two skin sites and records the response at each. The time gap between the two responses removes fixed delays at the nerve ending and muscle. NCV is used for carpal tunnel syndrome, ulnar nerve problems, diabetic neuropathy and nerve injury after fractures. It is a standard part of nerve conduction studies.
prereq: You need: EEG and EMG recording for the origin and recording of muscle and nerve signals, and electrode theory for surface electrode behaviour.

blocks.text: Nerve conduction velocity (NCV) is the speed at which an action potential travels along a peripheral nerve. The unit is metres per second (m/s). The instrument stimulates the nerve at two points on the skin and records the response from a muscle or from the nerve itself. Some syllabi call the whole test nerve conduction studies (NCS); this chapter covers the velocity measurement.

For a motor nerve, the recording electrodes sit over the muscle belly and tendon. The stimulator gives a short current pulse through surface electrodes. The muscle response is the compound muscle action potential (CMAP), a sum of many muscle fibre action potentials, usually a few millivolts (mV). For a sensory nerve, the recording electrodes sit over the nerve trunk. The response is the sensory nerve action potential (SNAP), a sum of sensory axon potentials, usually a few microvolts (μV). The SNAP needs more amplification and averaging because it is small.

Latency is the time from the stimulus to the start of the response, measured in milliseconds (ms). Amplitude is the height of the response. Latency tells when the signal arrives; amplitude tells how many fibres responded. Velocity uses latency and distance, not amplitude. Surface electrodes are safe and repeatable; needle recording is used only in special cases. Needle EMG analysis is in EEG and EMG recording. Stimulators used for therapy are covered under electrotherapy and nerve stimulators.

Stimulate the nerve at a distal site, far from the muscle. The latency you see at the recording electrode includes three parts: conduction from the distal stimulus site to the nerve terminal, the delay at the neuromuscular junction, and the time for muscle fibres to start their action potential. Call this common delay D. It is not nerve conduction along the long segment you want to measure.

Now stimulate the same nerve at a proximal site. The new latency equals D plus the time to travel the extra distance d between the two stimulation sites. Subtract the distal latency from the proximal latency. D cancels:
Δt = t<sub>proximal</sub> − t<sub>distal</sub>;  v = d / Δt
blocks.where: t<sub>distal</sub> and t<sub>proximal</sub> are the latencies from stimulus to response onset at the distal and proximal sites, in seconds (or milliseconds); Δt is their difference in the same unit; d is the distance between the two stimulation sites in metres (or millimetres); v is the nerve conduction velocity in m/s (or mm/ms). Because 1 mm/ms = 1 m/s, many machines report millimetres and milliseconds directly.

items: Place the recording electrode over the muscle for a motor study, or over the nerve trunk for a sensory study.
Stimulate the distal site. Increase the stimulus until the response stops growing; this is supramaximal, so all fibres fire.
Record the distal latency and amplitude.
Stimulate the proximal site with the limb in the same position. Record the proximal latency and amplitude.
Measure d with a tape along the nerve path between the two stimulation points.
Compute Δt and v = d / Δt. Repeat and average; note skin temperature.

blocks.text: Distance is measured between the two cathode positions, along the line of the nerve, with the joint at the same angle for both stimuli. A 10 mm error in a 200 mm segment changes v by about 5 percent; this is a common reason for a wrong answer. Record distance in millimetres.

Temperature changes velocity. A cool limb conducts more slowly because ion channel kinetics and membrane properties change. Warm the limb, measure skin temperature, and compare with the other side. The latency difference method removes the fixed distal delay, but cooling still changes the speed of the measured segment. Motor and sensory fibres also conduct at different speeds: sensory fibres are often faster, and the lab reports them separately.

The CMAP or SNAP amplitude is read peak-to-peak or from baseline to the first negative peak, depending on the lab. Low amplitude with near-normal velocity points to axonal loss. Slow velocity with a preserved amplitude points to demyelination. Mixed pictures occur. This interpretation belongs to medicine. The instrument's job is to give a clean latency, a correct distance and a stable amplitude.

The nerve stimulator is a constant-current pulse source, so the current stays set even when skin resistance changes. A typical unit gives single rectangular pulses of 0.1–0.2 ms (up to 1 ms), 0–100 mA, at about 1 pulse per second. Its output is isolated from mains and earth, and each pulse also starts the recorder sweep, so latency is read from the stimulus mark.

The recorder is a bio-amplifier with high CMRR and a wide band, about 2 Hz to 10 kHz for motor studies. The stimulus artefact is large, so the amplifier must recover within a fraction of a millisecond; a ground electrode between the stimulating and recording sites keeps the artefact small. A muscle stimulator uses the same isolated output with longer pulses and pulse trains.

figure.caption: The worked example: the distal response starts 2 ms after the stimulus and the proximal one 6 ms after it. Only the 4 ms difference belongs to the 200 mm segment between the two sites, so v = 200 mm / 4 ms = 50 m/s.

spec.aria: A forearm with stimulation sites at the elbow and the wrist 200 millimetres apart and a recording electrode on the hand muscle; below, two muscle responses starting at 2 and 6 milliseconds, giving a 4 millisecond difference and 50 metres per second.

examples.question: A technician tests a motor nerve. The distance between the distal stimulation site and the proximal stimulation site is 200 mm. The distal latency is 2 ms and the proximal latency is 6 ms. Find the latency difference and the motor nerve conduction velocity. Give the velocity in m/s.
steps: Write the given values: d = 200 mm, t<sub>distal</sub> = 2 ms, t<sub>proximal</sub> = 6 ms.
Find the latency difference: Δt = t<sub>proximal</sub> − t<sub>distal</sub> = 6 ms − 2 ms = 4 ms.
Use the formula v = d / Δt. Keep mm and ms together: v = 200 mm / 4 ms = 50 mm/ms.
Convert to m/s. Since 1 mm/ms = 1 m/s, v = 50 m/s.
Check with SI units: d = 0.200 m and Δt = 0.004 s, so v = 0.200 / 0.004 = 50 m/s. The answer agrees.
examples.answer: The latency difference is 4 ms and the motor nerve conduction velocity is 50 m/s.
examples.check:
d_mm = 200
t_distal_ms = 2
t_proximal_ms = 6
dt_ms = t_proximal_ms - t_distal_ms
v_m_per_s = d_mm / dt_ms
print(dt_ms)
print(v_m_per_s)

traps: Using the proximal latency alone gives v = d / t<sub>proximal</sub> = 200 / 6 = 33.3 m/s, which is too low. Use the latency difference Δt.
Mixing units: 200 mm / 4 ms is 50 mm/ms, which equals 50 m/s. Do not divide millimetres by seconds without converting.
Measuring distance from the stimulation site to the recording electrode instead of between the two stimulation sites gives a meaningless velocity.
A cool limb slows conduction. Record skin temperature and compare with the other side before trusting a low velocity.
CMAP or SNAP amplitude does not enter v = d / Δt. A small amplitude changes the diagnosis, not the velocity arithmetic.

quiz.q: Define latency in a nerve conduction study.
quiz.a: Latency is the time from the stimulus to the onset of the CMAP or SNAP, measured in milliseconds.

quiz.q: State the difference between CMAP and SNAP and give their usual units.
quiz.a: CMAP is the compound muscle action potential recorded over muscle, usually in mV. SNAP is the sensory nerve action potential recorded over a nerve trunk, usually in μV.

quiz.q: Why is the distal latency subtracted from the proximal latency?
quiz.a: The distal latency contains the common delay D from nerve terminal to muscle activation. The proximal latency contains the same D plus conduction along the extra segment. Subtracting removes D and leaves only the time for the measured segment. In a sensory study there is no neuromuscular junction; the subtracted part is the conduction time in the distal segment plus any fixed recording delay. The subtraction idea is the same.

quiz.q: The distance between two stimulation sites is 150 mm. Distal latency is 1.8 ms and proximal latency is 5.8 ms. Find the nerve conduction velocity.
A student reports 33.3 m/s for d = 200 mm, t<sub>distal</sub> = 2 ms and t<sub>proximal</sub> = 6 ms. What mistake was made and what is the correct value?
quiz.a: The student used the proximal latency alone: 200 / 6 = 33.3 m/s. The correct method uses Δt = 6 − 2 = 4 ms, so v = 200 / 4 = 50 m/s. Using one absolute latency leaves the distal delay in the calculation.

quiz.q: A constant extra delay of 1 ms, common to both responses (for example from the recording system), is added to both latencies. What happens to Δt and to the calculated velocity?
quiz.a: Δt is unchanged: (6 + 1) − (2 + 1) = 4 ms, so the calculated velocity is unchanged. This works only for a delay common to both responses. Real cooling slows the fibres in the measured segment, so Δt and v do change — warm the limb and record skin temperature.

quiz.q: Why does the test use supramaximal stimulation?
quiz.a: Supramaximal stimulation makes all available nerve fibres fire. The response then does not grow with small changes in stimulus strength, so latency and amplitude are stable and repeatable.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern NCV systems combine stimulator, amplifier and automatic cursor detection in one box, and some use wearable surface arrays for longer recordings. Research groups are testing ultrasound-guided stimulation and machine-learning help for reading traces. Intraoperative monitoring uses the same latency idea to warn of nerve injury during spine surgery.
